bio.en: Kunal Shah is the founder and CEO of CRED, the Indian fintech app for credit-card bill payments, and a widely followed thinker on why products succeed in India.
bio.zh: 库纳尔·沙阿（Kunal Shah）是 CRED 的创始人兼 CEO，CRED 是一款印度信用卡还款金融科技应用，他也是关于"产品为何能在印度成功"的广受关注的思考者。

summary.en: Kunal observes that many top global CEOs were India-born immigrants who faithfully scaled their founders' "dharma," or core principles. He argues Indian users relate to time and money differently - for instance, no Indian has been paid by the hour. The episode is a fascinating lens on building products for the Indian market and its distinct cultural logic.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH

Let's say for example, lots of engineering graduates come from only a few countries because society was bent towards early exposure to mathematics.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: I'm generalizing here, but that's the classification.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And the third is Vishnu, the God of sustenance.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And their avatars-the word “avatar” comes from Vishnu who keeps changing avatars.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: So we have Rama, Krishna, all these Gods are avatars of his.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: So what you notice is that if you take a two by two of people who are high on values and low on values, are high on obedience and low on obedience, you make an interesting two by two.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: Now, Lord Krishna, who is one of the very popular avatars, which suits the entrepreneurial category, is high on values but very low on obedience. He was known to be the naughty God and he could actually create lots of things.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And there is Rama, who is known to be the one who follows principles and is obedient.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: So they will follow ‘dharma’ and scale on that.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And then there are these notorious characters, there is Ravana who is low on values, low on obedience, and there is Duryodhana which he says that he is high on obedience but low on values.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: So these are the people that you don't want to be.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And what you notice is that a lot of CEOs have done well because they follow the ‘dharma’ of the founders quite well.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: They have not diluted the dharma of the founders who have started these companies, and managed to sustain that.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And a lot of CEOs have this need to say, "Oh, I'm going to change the company forever and it'll be my identity and I will change the logo and I'll change the name and I will do all sorts of things."

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: But maintaining ‘dharma’, where I will say that “These principles were given to me and I'm going to sustain this and make it even bigger," comes from the humility of saying that there is something that was built with some pure form factor, and I think therefore that character stays on.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And therefore we have the characters of Brahma and Shiva, the founder and destroyer.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: That's the thing.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: But sustenance is the harder one.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And therefore our avatars keep happening over time and different hurdles come and then different levels come.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: But when you think about the archetype of, at least the Indian CEOs, I've seen that they are fabulous at moving between Krishna and Rama all the time.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: They can play this consistently, and therefore they keep evolving and keep making these companies bigger and bigger.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And I think we'll see a lot more of this in years to come, because now they have the role models of these individuals who have done well.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: But the key principle is that if you ask the founders, they will love these CEOs if they're around because they maintain the dharma.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: For example, what Tim is doing is maintaining the dharma of Steve Jobs because if he had tried to change the dharma of Steve Jobs and the values of the company, it's very hard to imagine it sustaining itself forever.

turns.en: Wow, what an answer.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so I love that and it makes a lot of sense that that's where your mind goes.

turns.en: Yes.

turns.en: So I think being long-term about that mindset, and that's why some cultures last for thousands of years, because of this need for everybody to be more long-term versus short.

turns.en: Because that'd be amazing if you can reduce the risk of starting a company or is it just that it happens and people get super in debt?

turns.en: I want to keep talking about India and how it's different and especially what may surprise people about the market, both building there and then how to build products that are successful in India.

turns.en: For example, my guess is that, I don't know if this data is public or not to talk about, my guess is that Meta would not have more than $3 or $4 per user per year monetization in India.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH

Therefore a lot of Indian founders who tried to copy the Western market saying, “I'm going to have a few hundred million users” make a terrible mistake because they will need to then go abroad to find their ARPUs to balance the act.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And I'm not saying that it'll not change in 10, 20 years, but the expectation that many global companies come over here saying that, “I'm going to have these tens of millions of users who start paying me as soon as I come”, for Spotify, for Netflix, or Amazon Prime for that matter has not panned out.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So one of my takeaways here is just when you look at a startup as an investor especially, and you see “We've got 100 million users,” don't treat that the same as say 100 million users in the US or other markets.

turns.en: One more thing is the value of time as a concept.

turns.en: And I was paid, I'm pretty sure it was hourly.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: So what happens is in a low trust country, and all developing nations are low trust by design, because the institutions are not strong enough to really, really take care of many things.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: What happens is there is concentration of trust.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH

turns.en: Even the US is like that.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: They're the names of people.

turns.speaker: KUNAL SHAH
turns.en: And therefore in India, trust still comes from a lot of names of people who had a lot of trust behind them and reputation behind them.
